Long-toed salamanders (Ambystoma macrodactylum) inhabiting alpine lakes in the northern Rocky Mountains exhibit a remarkably protracted larval period. Field surveys of newly hatched individuals reveal that neonates emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a minuscule body size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This meager starting mass, which is derived from an egg diameter of roughly 2 millimeters in related ambystomatids, underscores the substantial growth trajectory that must be completed before metamorphosis. Juveniles typically undergo metamorphosis only after attaining a snout-vent length of 2.7 centimeters , a size threshold that is often not reached until after two full seasons of aquatic larval development. The high-elevation ponds these salamanders occupy are characterized by cold water temperatures and abbreviated growing seasons, factors that slow the accumulation of body mass and extend the pre-metamorphic interval relative to low-elevation conspecifics.

Sexual maturation in this species is preceded by a prolonged juvenile phase on land, during which individuals continue to feed and grow. Puberty is initiated only after juveniles achieve a snout-vent length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a milestone that marks the onset of gonadal development. This length at puberty represents a substantial increase from the metamorphic size, reflecting the considerable energy investment required to build the body reserves necessary for successful reproduction. Across the species' range, the snout-vent length at puberty shows moderate geographic variation, with individuals from colder, high-elevation sites tending to mature at slightly larger body sizes than those from warmer lowland populations. The onset of reproductive activity is tightly coupled to reaching this critical body length, after which individuals are capable of participating in the spring breeding migrations that are characteristic of this ambystomatid.

Female Long-toed salamanders exhibit a distinctive pattern of reproductive investment that is closely tied to body size. The ultimate wet weight attained by reproductively mature females is approximately 15.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 15.7 grams], a value that represents the maximum body mass recorded for adult females in the wild. Achieving this adult mass requires several years of terrestrial foraging on invertebrates, during which females accumulate the lipid stores necessary for egg production. The transition from a recently metamorphosed juvenile of just a few grams to a gravid adult female weighing over fifteen grams is a striking example of the resource-driven growth that typifies this species. Comparisons with congeneric species such as the tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum) indicate that Long-toed salamander females are among the smaller-bodied ambystomatids, yet their reproductive output remains considerable relative to their size.

Reproductive rates in Long-toed salamander have been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions that approximate the thermal regime of their natural breeding ponds. At a constant water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], females deposit between 90 and 411 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 90 and 411 eggs per clutch], producing a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually]. The resulting annual reproductive output is approximately 411 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 411 eggs per year]. The substantial variation in clutch size is likely attributable to differences in maternal body condition, age, and the availability of prey resources during the preceding foraging season. This pattern of producing a single, large clutch per year is common among temperate-zone ambystomatids and contrasts with the multiple-clutch strategies observed in some tropical salamanders. The annual reproductive output is consistent with a slow life-history pace, where females prioritize the quality and size of individual offspring over the production of numerous clutches within a single breeding season.

The lifespan of Long-toed salamander has been estimated from long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in stable pond habitats. Under field conditions that include a mean annual water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for individuals of this species is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This lifespan is remarkably long for an amphibian of its body size, particularly given the high metabolic demands associated with an active foraging lifestyle. The ultimate snout-vent length achieved by the oldest and largest individuals in these populations is 8.9 centimeters [Li = 8.9 centimeters], representing the asymptotic body size that few adults ever attain due to the constraints of predation and seasonal resource limitation. This combination of a decadelong maximum lifespan and a modest adult body size places the Long-toed salamander at the slow end of the life-history continuum for pond-breeding ambystomatids, where delayed maturity and extended reproductive windows are favored under cold, unpredictable environments.
